doc.title: Lonnie Liston Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 9, 2021

title: How Astral Traveling was written and named
summary: Seeing a Fender Rhodes for the first time in Pharoah's session, he found the twelve-bar cosmic blues and named it for astral projection.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: C 7, back to the F sus. And do you know, I call it, it’s a twelve bar, I call it the twelve bar cosmic blues. Oh man, it just came. We were in the studio out there and I had never seen a Fender Rhodes. So I asked the engineer — before that I played all the grand pianos. So you know the grand piano you don’t have to do anything. So I said, “Well what is that?” So the engineer said, “That’s a Fender Rhodes.” I said, “Wow, I never played it.” So everybody else are unpacking instruments, setting up drums. So I walked over and started messing with the knobs and Monk, it just came and it turned out to be, you know a twelve bar blues but the different voicing. Because you know regular blues is nothing but a 1-4-5
Then it’s C. But this one, you know

So that was, and man they ran over and said, “Man what was that?” I said, “I’m writing this song.” “Oh we’ve got to record that right now, and so what are you going to call it?” And I was studying at that time, astral projection you know, how if you eat right and meditate you can leave your body and be floating all over the world. I said okay since
we’re traveling all over the world, let’s call it “Astral Traveling.” And that’s what happened.
